The consumable that decides your yield

A nozzle is 15 grams of plastic, ceramic or rubber - and it carries your whole placement yield

Feeders, programs and operators all get attention. The tip that actually touches every component usually gets cleaned late and replaced later. These are the three failure patterns we are asked to fix most often on SIPLACE-style lines.

01

Mis-picks and skewed placements trace back to the tip

A worn bore, a chipped ceramic edge or a hardened rubber lip changes the vacuum column and the contact geometry. The first symptoms are small: an occasional miss, a rotated 0603, a rework that nobody blames on the nozzle. By the time the line flags it, hours of CPH are gone. The maintenance manual is blunt about the mechanism - dirt and wear are removed with a brush and compressed air, and nozzles out of spec are replaced, not negotiated with.

02

OEM lead time and price hit a consumable you replace on schedule

Nozzles are listed as wear parts in the X-series manual, alongside filter disks and hoses. Wear parts are a budget line, and a budget line should have a second source. We cross-reference by item number - the 0034xxxx and N610xxxx codes printed in the catalog and in your purchase history - and quote against the same geometry, not a guess.

03

Odd-form parts have no catalog answer at all

Transformers, E-caps with sleeves, brackets, connectors with locking clips: the datasheet stops at the standard tip sizes. That is where design and manufacturing starts - a gripper or suction geometry drawn around the component, checked on your head, then documented like a catalog part so the next engineer can reorder it.

From reject photo to packed order

How a Siemens nozzle order is actually built

Nine steps, each one leaving a document. The point is not speed alone - it is that every claim on this page can be traced to a datasheet, a manual section or a test you can repeat.

01

Component and head survey

You send the component (code, package, photos), the placement head (12-star, C&P20A, CPP, TwinHead) and the symptom. Head type fixes the shank, the collet seat and the changer behaviour before anything else.

02

Item-number cross-reference

We match your code against the special-nozzle catalog (0034xxxx, 030xxxxx), the ASM/Siemens tables in our supplier booklet (900 and 1000 series for 12-head and 20-head) and the manual's wear-part list (20xx, 28xx, 7xx, 9xx, 10xx, 12xx, 30xx).

03

Material and geometry selection

Vectra liquid-crystal polymer bodies for the special versions, with aluminium, steel, POM, PA6.6 or ceramic tip inserts depending on abrasion and weight. Rubber and PU tips for large or delicate parts - the catalog itself carries restrictions such as 'for rubber tip 12U1, 12U3'.

04

Machining and moulding

Standard geometries are produced from the documented dimensions; custom tips are drawn, approved, then cut. Bore, cone angle and seat are the three features that decide whether a nozzle picks like the original.

05

Functional test

Vacuum draw-through, bore clearance against the datasheet (a 731 is Ø0.9 mm with a 1.2 mm slot), and runout on a mandrel. The manual's own rule applies to our parts too: no bulk cleaning, no tips knocked against metal.

06

First article on your head

A sample runs on your machine, in your program, on your component. Pickup rate and miss records are the acceptance sheet - not a laboratory certificate that never saw a feeder.

07

Batch with identification

Production batches carry the item code and the colour-ring convention you already use on the 900-series parts, so the magazine slots load without retraining the operator.

08

Kitting to head layout

Nozzles arrive in rack or magazine-ready sets matched to your head layout, with the cartridge-rack and cleaning-box tooling listed in the manual available in the same order.

09

Wear review and replenishment

After the agreed interval we review your miss data and set a reorder point. Nozzle life is not published in the supplied documents - so the interval comes from your line, not from a brochure.

Steps 5 and 6 follow the checks printed in the SIPLACE X-series maintenance manual; where a value depends on your machine configuration it is confirmed with you, not assumed.

Fit and care

The maintenance sequence the manual itself prescribes

Six steps from section 4.7 of the SIPLACE X-series manual, written for nozzles. Follow them and a requalified nozzle behaves like a new one; skip them and no supplier can save the placement yield.

STEP 1

Prepare safely

ESD protection on (the manual ships an ESD wriststrap with the service box), head parked, hood secured per your machine procedure.

STEP 2

Set down in the changer

'Set the nozzles down in the nozzle changer' - manual 4.7.3. Never pull live nozzles out of a running head.

STEP 3

Brush, no bulk

CAUTION in the manual: do not clean nozzles in bulk. Apply slight pressure and move the brush back and forth to lift partially dissolved dirt.

STEP 4

Blow through

Compressed air through the bore, then return each nozzle to its magazine slot or cartridge rack - tips hanging free.

STEP 5

Ultrasonic only for ceramic

Distilled water in the bath; only the ceramic tips enter the fluid by about 2 mm; level within ±2 mm of the prescribed height. Fill and tooling per manual 4.7.4.1.

STEP 6

Verify before reload

Vacuum check and a short pickup trial on the head. A nozzle still out of spec after cleaning is a replacement, not a second wash.

ESD wriststrap 00320279-xx Cartridge rack 10xx 03071700-xx Cleansing tissue 00315253-xx Lint-free cloth 03082092-xx Distilled water + compressed air Universal head stand 00363290-xx

Part numbers are the manual's own service-box codes, quoted so you can check the tooling you already own. We are not affiliated with ASM; codes appear here only to identify the maintenance context.

Field notes

Eight articles on nozzles, yield and spare-part discipline

Written for the engineer who owns the placement line at 2 a.m. - each one ends with a step you can take this week.

ARTICLE 01The mispick that costs the whole shift starts at the tip

Missed pickups rarely announce themselves - they leak CPH one board at a time, and the nozzle is usually the last suspect.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

Somewhere on your line a placement head is missing one pickup in four hundred, and nobody has blamed the nozzle yet. That is the normal state of nozzle wear: it hides inside the noise of the line until the rework station starts queueing.

The first thing operators do is re-seat the feeder. The second is re-teach the pickup height. Both are reasonable, and both leave the actual suspect - a tip with a worn bore or a chipped ceramic edge - back in the magazine, picking the next four hundred components.

Make the tip part of the miss-rate investigation, not the last resort. Pull the nozzle for the failing position, hold it against the datasheet fields: bore diameter, slot width, tip face, seat. Compare against a known-good part from the same series. Nine times in ten the difference is visible before you measure anything.

That comparison only works if you have a known-good reference and a supplier who quotes by the same fields. Our match sheets carry the item number, the changer field and the tip geometry from the catalog page - so the spare behaves like the part you already trust.

Once a position is flagged, keep a record: nozzle code, head, hours, failure mode. Two months of that log tells you your real service interval - the number no manual publishes for your line.

Next shift, pull the nozzle for your worst-performing position and photograph it next to a new one. If you cannot tell them apart at arm's length, send both photos to info@smthelp.com - the first read is free.

ARTICLE 02Vectra, ceramic or rubber: reading a nozzle datasheet like an engineer

Five fields on one catalog page tell you more than a supplier's brochure - if you know what each one constrains.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

Open any page of the 7xx/9xx special-nozzle catalog and you get five fields: item number, name, material, restriction, changer handling. Most buyers read the number and skip the rest. The rest is where the engineering lives.

Choosing by part number alone means inheriting someone's 2004 material decision for a component that may not exist any more - and paying for it in misses when the tip hardens, the insert wears or the body cracks.

Read material as a duty statement. Vectra liquid-crystal polymer bodies are stiff and light, which suits fast star-head cycling. Steel or aluminium inserts change how the tip face wears. PU and rubber tips win on delicate or irregular parts but are consumables on a schedule. Ceramic resists abrasion but hates being knocked - which is why the manual bans bulk cleaning.

When we cross-reference, the material field is a conversation, not a copy. Same number, better insert for your component - or the documented original if your process is tuned to it. The datasheet page you send is the drawing we quote against.

Keep the catalog pages for the nozzles you actually run as a one-page per position reference. When the next engineer joins, the material decision travels with the part, not with one person's memory.

Send us a catalog page number and your component code; we will return the material read and what we would change - no obligation to buy anything.

ARTICLE 03Why the 12-star head makes nozzles a line problem, not a shelf problem

One star, twelve or twenty tips, one changer: the geometry of the head decides your spares policy.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

A 12-star head turns twelve nozzles as one instrument. When one tip drifts, the machine does not tell you which one - it just stops hitting its numbers.

Lines with star heads treat nozzles as individual parts and spares as a drawer of loose tips. The head disagrees: it grades the set. A single mismatched seat, and the changer, the vacuum test and the placement record all conspire to hide the cause.

Buy and store nozzles as head sets. Full set of spares per head, matched to the same series and changer behaviour; magazine slots labelled to the head layout; one position changed at a time so the miss-rate data stays readable. The manual's own procedure - set the nozzles down in the changer - assumes exactly this discipline.

Our kitting is built for it: spare sets per head family, colour-ring conventions that match what is already on your shelf, and changer handling stated on every line of the quotation, because 20 of the catalog's 128 pages say it differently.

Quarterly, rotate the set: the positions with the highest pickup counts come off first. Within a year your own records show which geometries wear fastest on your components - and your purchase orders get smaller and smarter.

Tell us your head type - C&P6/12, TwinHead, C&P20A or CPP - and we will send the spare-set sheet for that family.

ARTICLE 04Never bulk-clean a nozzle: four rules printed in the ASM manual

The maintenance chapter is blunt about cleaning. Follow it and nozzles requalify; ignore it and you are buying failures.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

The maintenance manual for the SIPLACE X series devotes a full section to nozzles, and one line in it is printed as a CAUTION: do not clean the nozzles in bulk.

Every shortcut in nozzle cleaning is a future placement defect with a delay. Tips knocked against a metal tray edge chip invisibly. Bulk baths grind dirt across bore faces. A nozzle that looks clean and picks wrong is worse than a dirty one you flagged.

The manual's four rules are simple enough to laminate: one, set the nozzles down in the changer before touching them; two, brush with slight pressure, back and forth, never in bulk; three, blow through with compressed air and return each nozzle to its rack; four, ceramic only in the ultrasonic bath, distilled water, tips about two millimetres into the fluid, level within two millimetres of the mark.

We sell against those rules, not around them: cleaning boxes, cartridge racks and the S-6200 / SCM24 automatic cleaners run the same discipline on a schedule, so the midnight brush session - where most chipping actually happens - disappears.

Put the four rules on the cleaning bench. Track one month of nozzle damage found during cleaning; when the number drops, the discipline is paying for itself.

If your current cleaning routine is not written down at all, ask us for the one-page version we ship with every nozzle order - free, with our compliments.

ARTICLE 05Cross-reference before you quote: from worn part number to solved order

A worn nozzle is a document exercise - item number, head, component. Here is the checklist we run.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

A worn nozzle arrives at a supplier's desk as a photograph and a hope. It leaves as one of three answers: exact match, functional match, or 'send the sample' - and the good suppliers say which one they are giving you.

Buyers have been burned by the silent version of this: a part that fitted the head, fought the changer, and quietly cut pickup yield for a month before anyone connected the two events.

Cross-reference is a checklist, not a favour. Item number from the body or purchase history; head model and firmware generation; the changer-handling field; the component and package being placed; the failure mode you are actually solving. Five inputs, and a quotation can be honest.

This is the whole front door of our shop. The catalog, the manual wear tables and our own booklet are the three registers we run your number through - and the answer comes back as a match sheet with the tier stated: 50, 90 or 100 percent.

When the match sheet is right, reordering becomes a part number and a quantity instead of a negotiation. Keep the sheet with the datasheet copy from article two.

Send five item numbers from your crib sheet and we will return five match lines within a day - that is the cheapest proof of this process you will ever get.

ARTICLE 06Odd-form parts do not fit standard tips - how custom geometry gets built

When the catalog stops, real engineering starts: sample, drawing, first article, documentation.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

The catalog ends at the standard tip. The component in front of you - the transformer with the clip, the connector nobody has ever fed automatically - starts where the catalog ends.

Teams try to force odd-form parts onto catalog nozzles. It half-works, and half-works on a placement line means full-price downtime with a mystery cause.

Custom geometry follows a fixed sequence: sample in hand, contact points mapped, suction or grip chosen for what the part can actually tolerate, drawing issued, first article run on your head, and only then a batch number. The output is a documented part - because an undocumented custom tip dies with the engineer who made it.

That sequence is our namesake capability: the booklet's custom pages, the gripper families for E-caps and chucking parts, and the Φ8.0 / Φ10.0 rubber rows all began as somebody's odd-form problem. Every one ends as a datasheet you can reorder against.

The next time an 'impossible' component shows up in RFQ, the custom file already has reference families to start from - and your engineering notes are in the same folder.

Photograph the part that will not place, note its head, and send it over. The first geometry read costs nothing.

ARTICLE 07The silent tax on your placement line: worn nozzles and lost throughput

Nobody budgets for a fifteen-gram consumable - which is exactly why it quietly owns your OEE.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

Nobody budgets for a fifteen-gram nozzle. Everybody absorbs its costs - in rework, in slow cycles, in the head that stopped at 2 a.m.

The visible nozzle bill is tiny next to its shadow: the stoppages it causes, the yield it quietly takes, the emergency air-freight when the one supplier with stock raises the price.

Price the consumable against the hour it owns. A line-hour of placement downtime costs more than most heads' full nozzle sets. Once you see that ratio, the question stops being 'are nozzles cheap' and becomes 'is my nozzle supply engineered' - correct storage, scheduled cleaning, a second source with a documented match.

This is what a nozzle programme from us actually is: matched sets, changer-stated quotations, cleaning tooling, and a wear review that feeds your own line data back into the next order. The unit price is only the first line of it.

Run the review every quarter and the programme compounds: fewer emergency buys, tighter intervals, and a spares budget you can finally forecast.

Open the cost model on this page, enter your own numbers, and see what your current setup is really worth - then send us the result and the item list together.

ARTICLE 08Identify, verify, replicate: buying nozzles without gambling

The three-step matching routine that turns a second source from a risk into a procurement policy.

Article bodies are published in English; summaries are translated.

A second source feels like gambling the first time: what if the parts are different and the line knows within a week?

Most sourcing pain is not price - it is the inability to prove the part is the same before the machine finds out the hard way.

Identify, verify, replicate. Identify: item number, head, changer field, component - the five-input checklist from the cross-reference article. Verify: a first article on your head, your program, your component; the pickup record is the acceptance certificate. Replicate: the approved geometry becomes a batch under one code with the match tier printed on the order.

The three-step routine is exactly how our nozzle orders run, and it is why we push the trial quantity first even when it is less money today. A verified 50-piece trial is worth more than an unverified pallet.

After the first cycle, reorders are one line: code, quantity, tier. The gambling is gone, and the supplier relationship becomes arithmetic.

Start with one position - your worst miss-rate head. Send the item number and the head model; we will return the identify sheet before asking for any money at all.

Straight answers

Questions buyers of Siemens nozzles actually ask

Which Siemens / ASM heads do you cover?
The 12-star head families (C&P6/12 and TwinHead per the X-series manual), the C&P20A star with 20 nozzles, and CPP continuous-pickup segments. The special-nozzle catalog we work from documents 7xx/9xx versions for the 12-star head; ceramic and plastic families 10xx, 12xx, 20xx, 28xx and 30xx are matched per your configuration.
What do you need from me to quote?
The best case: the item number from your purchase history or the nozzle body. Otherwise a photo of the nozzle in the magazine, the head model, and the component it places. Five minutes of your phone camera replaces a week of guessing.
Do you match OEM part numbers exactly?
We match geometry and function, and we say which tier you are buying: 50 % match (functional equivalent), 90 % (dimension-for-dimension on the datasheet fields), or 100 % (documented replica including changer behaviour). No supplier should quietly sell you the first tier at the price of the third.
Plastic, ceramic or rubber - how do I choose?
The documents make the map: Vectra LCP specials with PU/Alu/Steel/POM/PA6.6/ceramic inserts dominate the 7xx/9xx catalog; the manual's cleaning tooling is built around ceramic families; the booklet's rubber rows serve large components (Φ8.0, Φ10.0). Abrasive parts favour ceramic; delicate or irregular parts favour rubber and custom tips.
Can your nozzles run through the automatic nozzle changer?
108 of the 128 catalog datasheets state 'Handling with Nozzle Changer: Yes'; the rest carry a restriction or a 'No'. We quote the changer field explicitly for every position, because a nozzle that fights the changer is worse than no spare at all.
How do I make nozzles last longer?
Run the manual's own discipline: no bulk cleaning, brush with slight pressure, blow through, ceramic only in the ultrasonic bath with distilled water at the prescribed level (tips about 2 mm in, ±2 mm tolerance), and a vacuum check before reload. Scheduled nozzle cleaning is cheaper than an unplanned head stoppage.
Do you also supply the cleaning equipment?
Yes - the S-6200 full-automatic nozzle cleaning machine and the SCM24 auto nozzle cleaner, with manuals on the document server. Many customers bundle the first nozzle order with a cleaning schedule so the spares stay in spec.
What about price and lead time?
